Go safely!
Thank you for helping.

meanings.note: Bound noun often contracted to 거 in everyday speech.

examples.trans: This is my bag.

meanings.note: Used as honorific past retrospective (겪으셨던).

examples.text: 여기선 인터넷을 안 해서 몰랐어요, 저 때문에 곤란한 일 겪으셨던 거.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (adj).

examples.text: 암튼 내가 그날도 말했지만 공영방송에선 곤란해, 그런 옷.
examples.trans: Anyway, as I said that day too, an outfit like that is trouble on public television.
This expression comes from 'is problematic'.

괜찮다.gloss: to be fine; to be okay

meanings.en: to be fine; to be okay; to be alright
meanings.note: Used to reassure someone, decline an offer politely, or say something is acceptable.

examples.trans: I'm really fine.
Is it okay if we meet tomorrow?

meanings.note: Colloquial contraction of 그것

examples.trans: Where did you buy that?
That is a really good idea.

그동안.gloss: during that time, up to now

meanings.en: during that time, up to now
meanings.note: Used to reflect on a past period.

examples.trans: Thank you for everything up to now.
Have you been well during that time?

meanings.note: Colloquial contraction of 그런데; introduces a contrast or obstacle.
Used to shift the topic in conversation.

examples.trans: By the way, what time is it now?
I want to go. But I don't have time.
I want to wait right now.
How about trying to wait together tomorrow?

meanings.note: Used as connective -고 (꺾어놓고).

examples.text: 좀 곤란하긴 했지, 내 차 사이드미러도 다 꺾어놓고 수리비도 만만치 않게 나오고.
examples.trans: Well, it was pretty rough—they bent my side mirrors all the way back and the repair bill was no joke.
Let us do that (snapped back and) right away.

meanings.note: Plain first-person singular pronoun used with friends, younger people, or subordinates; contracts to 난 with -는 and becomes 내가 before -가.

examples.trans: I'm going to stay home today.
I'll go first.

meanings.en: to appear, be published, be achieved (a score/result)
meanings.note: Used for ratings, test scores, or results coming out

examples.trans: I came outside from the house.
The exam results came out well.

meanings.note: Placed before the verb it modifies.

examples.trans: I finished all my homework.
I ate all the rice.

meanings.note: Used for time or order.

examples.trans: Let's meet next time.
The next station is Seoul Station.

meanings.note: Takes a complement marked with 이/가.

examples.trans: I want to become a doctor.
It has already become 12 o'clock.

meanings.note: Usually followed by -e to mean 'because of'.

examples.trans: I was late because of the rain.
It's because of you.

meanings.note: Used as compound noun + -만 (렌틸콩만).

examples.text: 뭐 해주실 거예요? 저는 페타치즈랑 렌틸콩만 있으면 돼요, 아 퀴노아랑!
examples.trans: What are you making for us? All I need is feta cheese and lentils—oh, and quinoa!

examples.text: 아까 물어보니까 렌틸콩도 없고 치아시드도 페타치즈도 퀴노아도 없다고 해서 오늘은 어쩔 수 없이 먹는데요.
examples.trans: When I asked earlier, there were no lentils, chia seeds, feta cheese, or quinoa, so today I have no choice except to eat this.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (adj).

examples.text: 근데 준모한테 나는 만만하고 술친구 하기 좋고 편하고 딱 거기까지인가 봐.
examples.trans: Yet to Joon-mo, I am easygoing, a fun drinking buddy, and comfortable—and I guess that is as far as it goes.
This expression comes from 'easygoing, unintimidating and'.

meanings.note: Combines with 하다 in 말하다 (to speak, to say).

examples.trans: I don't know what you mean.
You speak Korean well.

meanings.note: Common verb for expressing thoughts in words.

examples.trans: Please speak slowly.
Speak loudly.
Did you hear about this head, brain?
I was busy today because of head, brain.

meanings.note: Everyday verb for eating a meal or food; honorific equivalent is 드시다.

examples.trans: Let's eat lunch together.
Did you eat breakfast?

meanings.en: to not know, to be unaware of
meanings.note: 르-irregular verb: stem 모르- + -아요/-았어요 → 몰라요 / 몰랐어요.

examples.trans: I don't know well either.
I didn't realize time was passing.

meanings.note: colloquial contraction of 무엇; also used rhetorically to brush off a question

examples.trans: What are you doing now?
Why are you even asking something like that?

meanings.note: Used as noun + locative (밑에).

examples.text: 밑에 김 실장님 기다려요, 가야 돼요.
examples.trans: Chief Manager Kim is waiting downstairs—I need to get going.

examples.text: 먼저 밑에 가 계시죠, 저는 신디 씨랑 할 얘기가 있어서요.
examples.trans: Please go wait downstairs first—there is something I need to talk over with Ms. Cindy.

meanings.note: Literal meaning: steamed rice.
By extension, refers to a meal in everyday expressions like 밥 먹다 ('to eat a meal').

examples.trans: Have you eaten?
Today's lunch is delicious.

보다.gloss: to see, to watch; to take (an exam)

meanings.en: to see, to look at, to watch
meanings.note: Primary meaning.
Idiomatic in 시험을 보다.

examples.trans: I watched a movie on the weekend.
I took the driver's license exam.

meanings.note: Used as past background (사놨는데).

meanings.note: Negative copula used with nouns (often with -이/가)

examples.trans: Oh come on, surely not—give him a call right now!

meanings.note: Short-form negation placed directly before verbs and adjectives

않다.gloss: to not do, to not be

meanings.en: to not do, to not be
meanings.note: Auxiliary negative verb/adjective used after -지 (long-form negation)

examples.trans: The weather isn't cold today.

없다.gloss: to not exist, to not have

meanings.note: Often used directly without a locative particle to mean 'here'.

examples.trans: Please sit here.

meanings.note: colloquially often pronounced/written 이쁘다

examples.trans: The flowers are really pretty.
This color is prettier.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (interj).

examples.trans: Yeah, she was pretty—and I asked her out for a second date too.

meanings.note: demonstrative determiner placed before a noun
